items.body:
Old pals Christina Vantzou and Félicia Atkinson reflect on coastal living on their first collaborative album, blending environmental echoes from Rome, Normandy and Hydra with mellow synth, piano, Rhodes, vibraphone, lap steel, gongs and spoken word, pulling us into the sublime.

The third chapter in RVNG's ongoing "Reflections" series, 'Water Poems' crystallises a creative relationship that began way back in 2009. Vantzou and Atkinson have performed together before, most notably in 2019 at Philharmonie de Paris, but this is the first time the duo have made a record together. Both artists live by the sea, Atkinson in Normandy on the French coast, and Vantzou in Greece, using that shared experience to power a series of hazy dream sequences filled with subtle gestures. "The sea was not taken as a monolithic postcard," Atkinson explains. "But more of a person; an energy, a mystery, a complex character we face everyday, as human beings living by the sea."

Indeed, the esoteric energy of the sea - its tides, force, majesty and hypnotic, mystical pull, is captured by the duo's eddy of electroacoustic treatments and bespoke natural soundscapes. They recorded the material in a factory on the island of Hydra in Greece, at Villa Medici in Rome and at home in their respective studios, adding expressive environmental recordings from Delphi and the Eftalou Hot Springs. The record plays like a single, hazed thought, ebbing and flowing through the same shallow waters. Words emerge and disappear into carefully processed sounds at first, before forming sentences and whole thoughts on the second side. "How can a body swim," Atkinson mouthes. "How can a person dream?"

Gorgeously, quietly seductive gear from two of the very best at this sort of thing, one to file next to Meitei's sublime 'Sen'nyū (泉涌)' from last year - recline and drift into it.

items.body:
Still influential three decades after its release, Rachel's' debut album is a low-key genre classic, welding the cinematic orchestrations of Carter Burwell to nascent post-rock structures and influencing bands like A Silver Mt. Zion and Clogs in the process.

Originally deployed on Touch And Go's sister label Quaterstick in 1995, 'Handwriting' was a complete anomaly at the time. There was a feeling that the album had only appeared on the label because it'd been the home of Rodan, the popular post-hardcore outfit that Rachel's founder Jason Noble had been a member of. But as time ticked on, Rachel's forward-thinking fusion of post-rock and chamber music began to appear more prescient. The band was originally conceived by Noble and viola player Christian Frederickson in the late '80s, but when Rodan blew up, Noble was too preoccupied to follow up their experiments. Time, of course, ticked on and Rodan imploded, so Noble and Frederickson picked up the pieces, inviting pianist Rachel Grimes to contribute. And the band's debut is a real one-off; they'd follow it with the brilliant Nyman-esque 'Music for Egon Schiele', but by that time their post-hardcore/post-rock echoes had all but disappeared. As it is, 'Handwriting' is at the root of a sound that almost immediately blossomed further north in Montréal. 

Linking the tangled riffs of Slint and of course Rodan with the scenic ambience of Labradford and, most importantly, Michael Nyman's minimal compositions, Noble, Grimes and Frederickson pre-empted something that's permeated throughout the scene at large over the three decades that followed. Even 'M. Daguerre', one of the album's early highlights and its jazziest track, that hews closer to The Necks' early material than anything else, provides a tangible blueprint. But it's the cooler, quieter moments that keep us coming back to 'Handwriting', like the emotive 'Seratonin' or the absolute milestone 'Full on Night', a stripped-to-the-bone Southern gothic post-rock jam that dissolves into a mass of radio static, film samples and chugging steam trains. If Godspeed hadn't heard this one before they recorded 'F♯ A♯ ∞', we'd be very surprised.

items.body:
Written for four Ebow-ed guitars, 'Avaeken' preserves a site-specific piece that O'Malley used to accompany an exhibition by Banks Violette. It's a microtonal symphony dedicated to Alvin Lucier and Kali Malone that's almost physically disorienting - RIYL Eleh, Phill Niblock, Pauline Oliveros et al.

It must be difficult to strike a balance when you're best known for creating some of the heaviest, most chest-pummeling drone music to ever vibrate from a stack of Sun amplifiers. But O'Malley's risen to the challenge; 'Avaeken' is relatively minimal, for him at least, but smacks with an intensity that you don't really see coming until your body starts feeling it. Made using four vibrating strings, he tunes the instruments to create that unsettling beating sound that seems to whirl around the noggin as the resonances interfere with each other. O'Malley wrote the piece following a commission from Belgium's ZWERM electric guitar quartet in 2020, performing it a handful of times before they knuckled down and recorded it in Gent's Muziekcentrum De Bijloke, a medieval hospital that's been fitted out with the proper acoustic treatments. 

And if you've been studying O'Malley's output carefully, you'll already know that he's frequently been spotted alongside Violette, the American artist best known for his huge sculptures and installations. The two have been friends for two decades at this point and have worked together multiple times, so when Violette was describing his show 'Wish You Were Here', an exhibition that tears at the fabric of America's subcultural underground, O'Malley immediately thought about this piece. The link might not be obvious, but O'Malley's use of phase cancellation - when "sound energy is eating itself", in O'Malley's own words - reaps ample rewards here. The effect is unsubtle, penetrating oscillations so disorienting that Violette's themes of societal rot emanate from every skewed tone.

O'Malley presents two takes of the same piece, fixing Violette's striking artwork - of a cracked mirror ball - to the cover. And it's incredible to hear him working as a composer for a change, letting the ZWERM quartet do the heavy lifting. Their expertise helps elevate the piece; it's precise, expertly rendered gear, the kind of thing you need to give your full attention to. Surprisingly, it's also got more in common with those Sunn O))) records than you might expect - play at high volume and you'll know exactly what we mean.

Recorded in 1991, 'Rise' sweeps up all known recorded material from A.R. Kane's Rudy Tambala and Cranes vocalist Alison Shaw, aka inrain, compiling a classic 7” for Rough Trade with additional, previously unreleased tracks. It’ll no doubt provide many with a first introduction to a prescient project by two scene legends, delving into shoegaze, dub, electro and trip-hop refractions of the highest order. It's the most essential Music From Memory release in a hot minute, crucial listening for all A.R Kane obsessives (that should be all of you) or anyone into Seefeel, Locust, Zurich.

For someone for whom Cranes' ‘Tomorrow's Tears’ and A.R Kane’s ‘Lolita’ are two absolute foundational texts, this reissue is basically something like a holy grail. Back in 1991, inrain appeared on Rough Trade's Singles Club series with a brief but brilliant 7" that sounded as if it'd been beamed in from another planet. A.R. Kane had already broken the mold, but these three tracks juxtaposed Shaw's dreamy vocals with dubby, spacious electronics and shimmering guitars in a way that wouldn't really rise to prominence until years later. Music From Memory do the heavy lifting here, remastering that original 7" from the original DAT tapes and adding the extra track 'Biology' and an alternate version of 'Sleep' to bump up the package. 

It's those original tracks that have us by the throat - we really can't believe they've been so slept on over the years. '...And Julie Rose' sounds like it should have been picked up for a Duophonic release a decade later, while 'Sleep' completely pre-empts Seefeel's 'More Like Space EP' that wouldn't appear for another couple of years. 

Prophetic, brilliant stuff.

Probably the biggest curveball in rap since Lil’ Bs ‘Rain In England’, Cities Aviv lands on Black Truffle with a set of psilocybin-infused dream sequences influenced by Jandek. Strange but true!​

Sticking out like a sore thumb next to Black Truffle’s usual lineup of avant, jazz, minimalist and electroacoustic pioneers and mavericks, Cities Aviv is the work of Wilbert Gavin Mays, who also records as African-American Sound Recordings, squeezing hip-hop conventions thru a chopped and screwed haze of “hermetic décollage”packed with fuzzy ambient interludes, loopy clouded reflections and stream-of-consciousness bars. 

Gavin Mays has always been on the perimeter of many scenes, happy enough to draw his own landscape while everyone else churned up the same old mud. That's truer than ever on his recent run, culminating in this brilliantly unexpected Black Truffle co-sign. Operating on his lonesome, Mays creates music that can't be pigeonholed - it's barely even rap. He spits on the two-part title track, but his words dilate awkwardly over noisy, new age synths and blown-out, pitch-screwed rhythms. They might not even be strictly on the beat at all, a mood that he prolongs throughout 'Even Colder Spring’, an album that in places sounds more like Seefeel than it does MF DOOM.

While Mays’ work can sometimes read claustrophobically bleak, the production here is surprisingly approachable; the instrumental ‘Martine Drift’ could almost be a snatch of Cluster’s Zuckerzeit caught through dial-up internet, and the distant drums of ‘L_area’ cross with lo-fi IDM, while closer ‘Final Heaven’ dissolves a cloud of loops thru almost seven minutes of ecstatic, rippling distortion. And as the label point out, the cover art is inspired by Jandek’s Corwood Industries label, which gives you some idea of where it's at.

items.body:
A Colourful Storm's Fleetway Tapes series follows classic entries from Time Is Away, Vladimir Ivkovic, Felix K, Young Sparks and others with a heart-stopping selection put together by Berlin-based film journo Florence Scott-Anderton, a fathoms-deep, laser-focused mix that doesn't come around often, engulfing high-art/low-culture TV samples with a series of cues excavated from film - think of it as a sort of Blockbuster Video nostalgia-tinted answer to Time Is Away's flawless thematic mixes.

Florence knows her shit. Not only does she provide words and sounds for MUBI's international film mag Notebook, where she's covered Tōru Takemitsu and crafted an ode to Derek Jarman, but she's a resident on NTS's ace Sounds on Screen. Nose through her archive and you'll find a deep dive into the sonics of lesbian cinema, an exploration of Aussie icon Nicole Kidman's filmography, a mix dedicated to Japanese vanguard Satoshi Kon, a history of the sounds of Iranian cinema and loads more (really, there's so much). And it's this same anti-hierarchal level of expertise and passion she brings to 'A Requiem for Prime Time', a very personal journey thru her memory banks that collages dialog samples, TV ambiance, art oddities and various soundtrack selections that eschew the usual narrative. We'll be honest, we've gotten pretty fatigued with the OST industrial complex and its parallel stream of repetitive, hyper-referential shovelcore outings from genre dorks whose interest in music peaked with 'Stranger Things'. Thankfully, Florence opts to sail down a completely different channel, not avoiding the mythologised synth wave completely (Simon Boswell's killer 'Hardware' cue 'It's Horrible... I Love It... What Is It?' shows up as a bonus like a peanut in caramel) but concentrating on dislocated, provocative and often completely overlooked sounds that drift far from the established "score bro" cult canon.

"It's not like you want to be an accountant," a muffled Australian voice narrates over ketamized SFX on the opening side. "You, like me, want something that is creative, that is out there a little bit." A clip from Peter Mullan's 2002 drama 'The Magdalene Sisters' appears, pulling us right back to that moment when trip-hop aesthetics bled into Hollywood's mainstream, and before long we’re riding a different train of thought, stitching cavernous twee rock with pastoral post-Glass minimalism and scratchy, evocative environmental recordings. Canned sax solos and airy guitar plucks fade into cuts from Mike Figgis's notorious experimental film 'Timecode', and somehow Woijciech Kilar's end credits from Francis Ford Copolla's 'Bram Stoker's Dracula' show up for some thematic relief. On the flip, Florence opens the side with waved, Eno-style psychedelic ambient that's ruptured by a beat isolated from Joe Delia's sordid score for Abel Ferarra's famously abhorred erotic thriller 'The Blackout'. From here, we're catapulted across Christophe Beck's 'Bring It On' soundscapes, a cloudy, sub-heavy ambient marvel from Brooklyn artist Alex Bienstock and even Joe Jackson's aborted theme for 'Mike's Murder', a 1984 Debra Winger vehicle that had its entire soundtrack replaced with a more palatable one from John Barry.

Really, we can't say enough about this one. If you've been following Scott-Anderton's mixes (if you want just one, we recommend her Krzysztof Kieślowski selection), you'll already know how vital her point of view is, but she takes us to a completely new zone with this one. It's a head-scratcher that'll have you wondering what it is yr actually listening to - a way to contemplate the Y2K era as it completely vanishes into popular mythology.

Revisiting their debut album '.After', Tujiko Noriko and Adrian Corker commission a suite of remixes, bringing in Koshiro Hino ov YPY, goat (JP) and KAKUHAN fame, Tashi Wada, DJ Trystero, Shojiro Nakaoka and DJ ojo to put their spin on the source material.

The original album only took Noriko and Corker a couple of days in the studio, but they wired the results to percussionist and arranger George Barton, who took it to the next level. They continue the thought on '.After Again', dishing out the stems to a carefully pruned list of collaborators - artists whose distinctive sounds only extend the original album's sonic universe. And of course it's the YPY version of the album's opening track 'Yasashii Sayonora' that'll have most of y'all chomping at the bit; Hino turns Corker and Noriko's source material to dust, time-stretching Noriko's vocal and zeroing in on the stuttering percussion and rusted turntable loops. Adding his signature jerks, he fills the track with clattering metallic clangs, twisting the voices into downsampled groans from a neighboring cyber-reality.

Tokyo's DJ Trystero opts for a different but similarly unique approach on his two reworks, the "All Frills" remix of 'Toku No Minato' and his "Naive Declension" version of the same track. On the former, he isolates almost indistinguishable elements of the original, setting the ghost traces to a typically deep, dubby groove and on the latter, creates a rugged, gear-heavy jam from the remains. It's actually Nakaoka who provides the weirdest - yet strangely most recognisable - versions, using his custom generative code to match Noriko's voice with whirring interference and warbling digital detritus.

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)', on a new pressing for 2026.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like HTRK were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down into the abyss, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the drums become clammier while Jonnine's vocals drift like ghostly vapour trail. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, it's as good as it gets.

The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

I can feel the waves is Frances Chang's debut on RVNG Intl.

"A boundary-pushing musician and multi-media artist from Brooklyn, New York, Frances Chang disrupts accepted reality through her unique and enchanting compositions. Chang’s songs are an exercise in communication, probing the tension between idiosyncratic personal experience and the drive to understand, and be understood, through a collective language.

For “I can feel the waves,” a piano-centric melody is ornamented with primitive electronics and poetic vocals. The track boldly demonstrates Chang’s strength for unconventional yet contagious songwriting, and pioneers a genre the artist refers to as “slacker prog”: roomy and playful, offbeat and occasionally jarring, brimming with spiritual and emotional resonance.

The b-side, “Marry,” is a rollicking yet laid-back composition, with undaunted wobbly kicks bubbling under pianistic textures until a dialogue, acted out between Chang and Sylvia Gorelick, takes the foreground in the final moments of the track. As the instrumental carries its freewheeling pulse forward, the conversation, inspired by films like Kenneth Lonergan’s Margaret and Catherine Breillat’s Fat Girl!, along with Broken Social Scene’s “Anthems for a Seventeen-Year Old Girl,” turns toward the relationship between internal subjectivity and the external necessity of “staying small.”

Where is Frances headed from here? A piano is at the center, synths and strings swelling around its shoulders. A little less tension, a lot more production. Some shadows will be encountered, some forgotten skeletons unearthed. Music excavated from the subtler, deeper layers of cerebral and shared experiences. Music that is truly its own."

Jeff McIlwain re-emerges from his production slumber to deliver more aural candy for the Ghostly family on this new Lusine album.

Further settling into his latter-day groove as a producer of well-polished pop-tinged electronics, the Lusine of nearly 20 years ago has not disappeared altogether, the mechanics of his early IDM, ambient and downtempo productions still drive the creative process on ‘Sensorimotor’.

There is a more introspective yearn to this album however, a sensation most apparent in the numerous vocal contributions from Jeff and his wife, Sarah McIlwain, along with Vilja Larjosto and Benoît Pioulard. The latter’s manipulated vocals feature on the sub-Burial, hushed flutter of Witness which is destined to get synced by the CSI franchise sometime soon.

The A-side locks off a signature strip of dread martial steppers tension in ‘Pess One’, pivoting ghoulish bass spectres around flintiest snares harking to his aces for BEB/A14, next to the drily ricocheting drums and halftime rolige of a title tune reminding of his input to the Ruffhouse trio with Karim Maas & Vega. 

His B-side gets ruder with the pugilist drums on ‘NRG-97’, swarmed with string stabs and voice-in-head motifs recalling SD’s ‘Technical Warfare’ and Boymerang missiles, and coming with the strongback crud in a properly cantankerous ‘Under Surveillance’.

Jospehine Foster's 2016 release "No More Lamps In the Morning" available again via Fire Records.

"Foster, on nylon string guitar, and husband Victor Herrero, accompanying on Portuguese guitar, together weave intimate readings of songs spanning Foster's songwriting career including selections from recent albums "This Coming Gladness" (2008) and "I'm a Dreamer" (2013) and back to Born Heller (2004). Foster's new route is a free, chromatic music, a tuneful montana of mind--an expansive harmonic space dominated by Rif mountain on the horizon. As highwater as the music is, as broad the stylistic palette of the musicians, the music really exists in service of the lyrics. Two of the songs on No More Lamps are poems by Rudyard Kipling and James Joyce given musical settings by Foster. The rest arguably are musical settings of her own poems strengthened in a fiery crucible of guitars (and on 2 tracks Gyða Valtýsdóttir's cello) in which dissonant notes bend and quaver as wirefork embers, dying without affecting the glowing tonal fire which unites contrary forces in a Moroccan speakeasy. She and Herrero have performed, for an audience of burros, concerts of Federico Garcia Lorca poems set to music. A music of wandering and a music of roots."

items.body:
The Original Motion Picture Soundtrack for Crime 101 by experimental electronic musician, producer and composer Blanck Mass (She Rides Shotgun).

"Thunderous synth soundscapes are paired with nuanced character-driven themes creating a multi-faceted backdrop to the intense thriller. The Amazon MGM Studios film directed by Bart Layton is set against the sun-bleached grit of Los Angeles.

Crime 101 weaves the tale of an elusive jewel thief (Chris Hemsworth) whose string of heists along the 101 freeway have mystified police. When he eyes the score of a lifetime, his path crosses that of a disillusioned insurance broker (Halle Berry) who is facing her own crossroads. Convinced he has found a pattern, a relentless detective (Mark Ruffalo) is closing in, raising the stakes even higher. As the heist approaches, the line between hunter and hunted begins to blur, and all three are faced with life-defining choices– and the realization that there can be no turning back.

On creating the music, Power says :

“Crime 101 was an incredible movie to have the opportunity to score. At the centre of the story is, of course, the heist. However, it very quickly became apparent to me that this was not any heist movie, but more a Noir which happens to have a heist in it. The central characters and how their lives become intertwined was more important than the action, in a way. This is high-octane in parts, of course, but what really drew me to this movie was the character development. Lou, Davis and Sharon are the beating heart. I wanted to ‘be with them sonically’ throughout. Both the tender and the furious needed to be sympathetic with one another”."

items.body:
One of electronic music's most influential recordings, back in circulation.

Most readers of these pages will know the story, but to indulge you with a recap, Gottsching was part of electronic krautrock heroes Ash Ra Tempel and in 1981, off the back of a Klaus Schulze tour, sat down one evening and dropped a continuous piece of music which would uncannily imagine the arc of dance music for a quarter of a century.

Early adopters in the Chicago and Detroit warehouses and mediterranean pleasure palaces must have thrilled to the balanced and continuous surging flow of the hour long piece - even over two sides the mix is perfect for building a club atmosphere and suggesting avenues for mixing, whilst using merely two chords throughout. the minimalism offsets the percussive splendour perfectly - several years later the tune was rediscovered and co-opted into the huge italo house smash Sueno Latino, which cemented its foundation in the burgeoning balearic scene of the time and proceeded through several spells of rapturous revival throughout the nineties, not least when figures like Carl Craig and Basic Channel issued their own radically different reshapes and remakes of the piece.

Very satisfying then to have this Gottsching sanctioned edition, where the game might truly be said to have begun in earnest. As they say on the august walls of the Hardwax emporium - buy or die.

More slick sophisti-pop from the CPH scene via GB aka Gustav Berntsen, kinda heavily reminds us of a Japanoise/ jazz fusion take on Sam Prekop’s self-titled alltimer with bits of Red House Painters, Steely Dan and Prefab Sprout in there too.

Berntsen was stationed in London when he was writing 'Herzprung' and began to collect copies of the infamous free rag Metro, that he cut to shreds to fix up the lyrical portion of the songs. Once he had this in check, the Danish singer-songwriter called up his most trusted collaborators and booked a week at a studio "in the Swedish wilderness", where he dubbed the songs live to 24-track tape, encouraging improvisation and collaboration. And there's certainly a knottiness to this material that's unique to Bernsten; like many contemporary Copenhagen-based operatives, he's clearly well versed in classic rock and pop, from Fleetwood Mac and Steely Dan to Chick Corea and Haruomi Hosono, but he doesn't stop at pastiche, instead bringing his own absurdities to the table. "The Simpson's Season Six," he calls out harmoniously on opener 'Adrenaline', interrupting a stop-start drum fill and riffs that wouldn't sound out of place on a Gastr del Sol record. 

It would be hard to label 'Herzprung' post-rock, but there's a sense that Berntsen has at least learned from the genre's Chicago-era excesses. He seems to be driven by a holistic understanding of pop; at their heart, his songs are impeccably written, yet he's also not interested in taking the clearest path. On 'Belly', his cool-headed harmonies and almost tropicalia-strength choruses are complicated by winding instrumental sections and a phenomenally atmospheric dip into tape-fuckt cosmic ambience, while the lengthy 'Shit River' is a slowcore anthem that Berntsen expands with a full choir and an arsenal of synths.

Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.

items.body:
Tyondai Braxton’s new album, his first full-length release since the recording of his 2022 symphonic work, Telekinesis, reveals itself as unlike what came before and marks the beginning of a new chapter with UK label Erased Tapes. First off, there’s a lot more music here, 70+ minutes of pure electronics and sound design. Plus, it’s divided in a way that’s out-of-step with the longer forms the 47 year-old composer/producer has previously imagined into being. Of the album’s 15 tracks, more than two-thirds are sub-five minutes.

"The album brings together mostly newer works alongside pieces composed across the past decade, some of which appeared previously as standalone releases. To fully represent the scope of this period, Braxton incorporates the Dia / Phonolydian (2022) and Multiplay (2023) singles into Splayed Werks, foregrounding the project’s long-form compositional arc. Along with “Salt Point” and previously unreleased commissioned works such as “4 Zones” (2018) and “K Space” (2021), these pieces were always part of a broader, evolving body of material. Here, they are re-edited as newer versions and remastered by the excellent Matt Colton at Metropolis Studios in London and woven into a continuous narrative. The result is not so much a compilation, but a record that traces its own lineage in real time: a body of work composed across years, now fully realized as a single, cohesive statement.

What the circumstantial facts can’t reveal is the social, in-real-life context of Splayed Werks, an expansive episodic work that plants a musical flag on a turbulent period, and on which darkness and ambiance, rhythm and light, instinct and precision, organic textures and messy playfulness all share space. These Werks take stock of a constantly evolving world, as well as the evolutions experienced by their creator.

It may be a perfect album for 2026, a time when the sonic landscape continues to fervently embrace increasingly radical hybrids, at once club soundsystem-ready, art-installation-leaning, and music-school-mediated. But also, importantly, intuitive and hand-crafted. It’s no stretch to say that Tyondai had a hand in building this world. His two decades-plus-long career has seen him co-found electronic prog-punk heroes Battles (which he’s described as “a laboratory that masqueraded as a band”); performing as a duo with Philip Glass; write numerous electro-acoustic and chamber commissions for celebrated American new-music ensembles such as Bang on a Can All-Stars, Alarm Will Sound, Third Coast Percussion, Brooklyn Rider, and Yarn/Wire; having his “part installation, part band” HIVE project appear at The Guggenheim Museum, Sydney Opera House, and a 3-night residency at Big Ears Festival; and deliver a series of technologically ambitious, at times orchestral works for lauded labels of electronic, experimental and future-music, Warp and Nonesuch Records.

Meanwhile, the world outside has also radicalized. Mechanisms behind the creation, promotion, distribution and broadcast of new experimental music have been violently disrupted, even as audiences for it have grown. In the post-COVID streaming age, juxtapositions like “popular” vs “underground,” and “album” vs “collection” vs “project” have been more in-flux than ever before. The volume and acceptance of previously neglected ambient and contemporary classical sounds has been tempered by a lack of critical context, seeded with algorithmic buffoonery and AI fabrication. Such tensions enlighten not just the make-up of Splayed Werks, full of music recorded between 2018-2025, but its relatively simple sonic-collage forms.

The Splayed shapes and structures have also been influenced by the transformations in Braxton’s personal life. That Tyondai is now a father may not come as a surprise, but the fact that the man who rebelled against his formal music-school education in the late-‘90s, has, in 2022 become a professor of music composition at Princeton University, does. This lifestyle change—a full-time academic gig, escaping the careerist hamster-wheel beholden to commissions and collaborations, a home studio as his own workshop and testing ground, with the desire to finish things and the perspective to not be precious about it—is also key to the album’s sound. Braxton’s time is his own, and his idea of what it means to be an artist in our time has evolved as much as the surroundings. This too is what Splayed Werks is about. It may be a cliché to call each ensuing album by a veteran artist their “most personal,” but it’s no stretch to say this one best reflects who Braxton is in 2026.

As a portfolio, Splayed Werks hews to the menu of a dance music meets minimalist electronic composition, a throughline that stretches from IDM absurdists like Aphex Twin and Autechre, to contemporary immersives like Mica Levi and Laurel Halo. (And, to a lesser degree, to Braxton’s comrades and occasional collaborators, Kieran “Four Tet” Hebden, Jeffrey Cantu-Ledesma and Ben Vida.) It’s a world in which the multitude of dirty rhythms strays far outside club-land’s big rooms—though one can imagine expert mixing hands and a world-class soundsystem transforming the dubwise lo-fi linearity of “Oslo” into a psychedelic wonder, while the interplay between the bass-synth and the constantly deviating shuffle on “UnFS” may qualify as a leftfield banger. And its composed beatless spaces have little to do with current ambient proclivities—the at-once aggressive and ecstatic, panning miniature, “Realistic Water” sounds like power Laraaji.

The spectrum of Braxton’s ideas and directions reveals a voracious mind at play, changing up without overcomplicating the proceedings. Two different pieces called (fittingly) “Multiplay” layer and connect skittering textures in beatwise whimsy, before giving way to a droning dread and organised noise; yet each is adorned with birdcalls to balance the synthetic with the pastoral. “Nimble FX” is also built on hyper-jittery stop-start rhythm lines, and great big cinematic synths. All this music feels fluid, seemingly ready to change in the moment rather than having been dependent on some grand design. Meanwhile, longer, older, more spacious compositions like “4 Zones,’ whose short parts assemble into a narrative-free sound design, and the closing “K Space,” whose chaotic ambiance gives way to what sound like Moog hits, are more grounded, their inclusion shaping Splayed Werks into a multidimensional space, instinctive in how it all fits together."

“Every record I’ve ever finished, I’ve been shocked with what it is. I’ve never known it was finished until it was. Then you get to learn about it retroactively. If I’ve done it right, the finished thing will feel like its own personality, its own being, its own vibe. [Splayed Werks] included.” - Tyondai Braxton

items.body:
On her third studio album, Brooklyn-based artist Frances Chang feels out the boundary between bedroom pop and lavishly orchestrated avant-experimentation, writing on a century-old grand piano and spiking her productions with jerky, unconventional electronic elements. The end result is somewhere between Aimee Mann and Cate Le Bon.

There's something unmistakably ramshackle about Chang's productions, but at the same time, it all sounds as if it's been meticulously planned. On opening track 'I can feel the waves', her voice never falters as it soars over casual phrases from her aging baby grand, but the it's the beats that immediately catch your attention, rupturing the calm with the momentum of a footwork demo. Chang's clearly an obsessive listener and it's this passion that lends her songs a breath of originality; they're classic in a sense, informed by Burt Bacharach, Chet Baker and Dionne Warwick, which actually makes sense. And where she takes the songs after they've been written is fascinating, building them out with instrumentation that's not exactly unexpected, it's just ever so slightly off-kilter. Those warbling strings on the ace 'Bad zen', or the buzzing micro-repetitions on 'Marry' - these sounds just nudge the material into a different zone and assert Chang's personality.

And as it develops, Chang's confidence grows. She's most successful when the guardrails are fully off - like on the brilliant 'No avatar'. Here, she latches her Robert Ashley-esque vocal lead to a wonky synth arpeggio that she follows with piano - or vice versa? The other instruments coolly fall into line: drums, bass and organ seem to flutter, flourish and fall at Chang's command, never quite going in the expected direction. Even advance single 'Auratones of Desire' makes more sense in context, its well-sculpted fusion of psych drum breaks, frittered farfisa organs and soft vocal affectations widening the album's reach considerably. Given it some time and attention for full reward.

items.body:
Carrier winds the rhythmic tension to breaking point on his 4th self-released 12”, flexing fine-tuned muscle memory and inch-tight production in acres of negative space across a trio of soundsystem phantoms that dance in the long shadow of D&B and broken beat science. Huge tip FFO Autechre, Burial, Photek, T++.

Now three years into a generational run of inspirational plates - including an AOTY ’25 with ‘Rhythm Immortal’ for Modern Love - Carrier’s core sense of discipline and restraint continues to yield peerless reward on ‘Thresholds’. A lifetime’s love of, and immersion in, fwd UK dance musics has prompted him to chase a particular dragon of syncopated swerve and cavernous psychoacoustics to logical, next-level depths diffusing that dread pressure with an adroit, tendon-twitching precision and tactility.

Carrier has been instrumental in reminding ravers what was lost when D&B went stadium and pop-chart scale over the past decades, daring to run against the grain, trust his instincts, to return a sense of mystery and bold experimentalism to what was once a thrilling paradigm. This new trio of cuts eke exquisite nuance from tweaked fundamentals, swivelling 2-step off the bone into smoky hall-of-mirrors reflections of ‘Cure’, and specialising in a razor’s edge, toes-off-the-ground sorcery in a recursive, wraithlike zinger, ‘Scout’ that dips to the sexiest, tongue-tip breakdown, beside the tantric, anticipatory chicanery of ‘Black Channels’ which finishes us off with an all-tension-no-release weapon for the ages.

items.body:
Joining the 4AD roster, NYC avant-rock four piece YHWH Nailgun unload an 11-minute clip of pure math-punk artillery, all demon-possessed vocals, screaming organs, angular riffs and byzantine rhythms. Think U.S. Maple, Battles, Captain Beefheart, Pere Ubu and Still House Plants blended with 'Scum'-era Napalm Death and you'll have some idea.

Deployed only moments after Drake dropped not one but three bloated sets of playlist-ready mall pop, 'Magazine' arrives like a cool breeze during a heatwave. See, it's common sense in the AI era to feed the algorithms more, not less, increasing your chances to snag that illusive viral hit by relying on pure volume. Not hampered by the limitations of the format (remember, the "classic album" was only 40-odd minutes because vinyl demanded it), artists and labels have been hedging their bets, packing records with collaborations, remixes and undeveloped ideas in the hope that one of them might end up getting even half the traction of AFX's seemingly throwaway 'QKThr'. YHWH Nailgun laugh in the face of this logic, not just challenging 2026's idea of what an album should be, but 1966's, too. If you thought '45 Pounds' was lean, 'Magazine' trims even more aesthetic fat, cooking down the meat of jazz fusion, prog, noise rock, post-punk and grindcore like it's Wagyu, searing it off and providing just an umami-rich shaving to taste.

The whole process is surprising because so many of YHWH Nailgun's references were already bloated. The prog rock era was when the double album became almost commonplace; 'Magazine' meanwhile could quite easily be crammed onto a 7" at 45RPM. And yet, they've only increased in power since last year. Opener 'Ghost of Love' does more in a minute-and-a-half than most tracks do in three or four times the duration, spinning Jack Tobias' carnivalesque, Farfisa-like synths around Sam Pickard's pliant drums like matted spiderwebs, but leaving just enough room for Zack Borzone's no-wave shouts and Saguiv Rosenstock's hacking fragments of melody. 'Stillness Blues' is shorter still and somehow packs even more in, assembling screamo brickwork over industrial strength bass rasps using Pickard's clattery start-stop patterns as the mortar. It's hard to say this stuff's exhausting - it's over before you've even really come to grips with it - but YHWH Nailgun have a way of drawing you back in, again and again, just to try and catch a whiff of what's actually going on. 

There's the Radiohead-like moan of 'Innocent Sigh', the Eli Keszler-does-Pere Ubu intensity of the minute-long 'Ballerina' and the title track, 35 seconds of breakneck beats, bleeps and shouted phrases that rudely cuts off before it's even had the chance to fully extend its claws. It's a shocker, an eccentric, hyper skillful, deeply original blur of influences and innovation that really does remind us just how punchy rock music can be.

The spirit of legendary film score composer Toru Takemitsu looms large over Kotaro Maruyama’s economical yet lush studies, ranging from sublime echoes of Japanese environmental ambient to beatific pulse poems edging on weightless Heinrich Mueller works.

"Composing primarily with the piano, Kotaro Maruyama creates music for a variety of visual media, including commercials and short films. Influenced by the composer Toru Takemitsu, he places importance on the “silence” and "ambience" of sound, aiming to create works where the music quietly depicts a scene.

Kotaro Maruyama's first solo album, "Vapor Curve," is constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer. Notably, he avoids the concept of harmony for a single tone, instead pursuing a unique "woven harmony" created by intricately layering multiple independent melodies. Using only the OP-Z, and recording everything in a single take without using a computer, Kotaro Maruyama's "Vapor Curve" is distinguished by its uncompromising production style. The minimalist melodies that are layered to create an ambient soundscape, along with the incidental noise that gives an organic texture to the inorganic electronic sound, showcase the raw appeal of sound that is imperfect."

Daria Lourd (Bored Lord) + her wife, vocalist Jaelynn Walls = DARLYNN on their debut shot of Jersey club meets ‘90s R&B, woozy garage house and vintage psych-funk flavours.

"Darlynn is an Oakland-based duo composed of Daria Lourd (aka Bored Lord) and her wife, vocalist Jaelynn Walls. Dyke Den is a lesbian love story about two creative individuals finding each other and themselves through effusive and contemplative sonic avenues. Created in their home over the course of two years, this album speaks to the journey of Daria and Jaelynn’s romantic relationship as well as their evolving combined creative impulses.

On Dyke Den, Darlynn display their influences – from Janet Jackson and Sly & the Family Stone, to Frankie Knuckles and Larry Levan – in a sophisticated, fully realized, and overtly queered fashion. Joyous dancefloor moments are abundant. Tracks like “Make Yr Move” and “Like A Summer” celebrate deep house vibes ala Alleviated Records, while sultry R&B moves are flexed on “Girl 2 Girl” and “Alright With Me.” But longing and yearning exist within this joyous arc, and the question arises: “How can I get you to love me?” More than an idealistic narrative of girl meets they/them, Dyke Den paints a portrait of love in all its multifaceted moments: the bids for commitment, the stagnation of years going by, the wormholes of desire. Yet the album maintains its thesis of hope. The sweet, layered harmonies of closing song “Love Letter” display the power of life partnership: “My whole life is a love letter to you.” Dyke Den features artwork by Hailee Va in a sleeve designed by Eloise Shir-Juen Leigh. Darlynn’s final declaration, “We are all creatures of desire, completely built for love.”s"

Influential Brum punks/post-punks Swell Maps captured in their snotty pomp, 1979, for the legendary John Peel Sessions - just a year before disbanding, and prompting everyone from Sonic Youth to Nirvana in their wake.

“Noisy, chaotic, and defiantly experimental, Swell Maps may not have found commercial success in their time, but their impact on music is undeniable. An inspiration to bands such as R.E.M., Sonic Youth, Dinosaur Jr., Pavement and Nirvana, with Kurt Cobain famously being a fan and often seen sporting a Swell Maps T-Shirt. A democracy within the confines of punk’s anything is possible, members Biggles Books, Jowe Head and brothers Nikki Sudden and Epic Soundtracks—helped shape the landscape of post-punk and DIY music. Now, for the first time in over 40 years, The John Peel Sessions brings together all three of their recordings for John Peel, a figure instrumental in championing their sound.

Formed in the early ’70s and fully realised by 1976, Swell Maps embodied the DIY ethos, launching their own label and self-releasing the jagged, frenetic debut single ‘Read About Seymour’ in 1978. Peel was an early supporter, playing their record as soon as it landed on his desk—a moment the band described as one of disbelief and elation. His regular airplay of their music helped solidify their cult status, and these sessions capture the raw energy, off-kilter melodies, and boundary-pushing creativity that defined them."

One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.

items.body:
Required listening for computer music freaks, 'Synthesized Voices' originally appeared in 1976, collecting innovative composer Charles Dodge's prophetic vocal experiments - recordings of Mark Strand's surrealist poems recreated on Bell Laboratories' uncanny synthetic speech tech. If you're into Anton Bruhin's deranged 'Speech Poems', this'll hit the spot.

You've got to applaud DINTE for the timing of this one. Right now, it's hard to tell what's a real voice and what's been cobbled together using LLM tech, Frankensteined from decades of scraped voiceovers and newsreels. Synthesized voices are stapled to short form content and used to provide an air of humanity to mass-generated robo-slop. And listening to Dodge's set of pioneering studies, it's remarkable how the technology has evolved in such a short period of time. In the early '70s, when Dodge began his investigations, heavily synthesised voices were terrifyingly mechanical, usually used to depict malign forces - just cop any of those vintage Doctor Who episodes that feature Cybermen. What's fascinating is that Dodge seems to understand its crucial limitation; he doesn't attempt to make the voice sound more human (and therefore more tolerable), but mirrors Strand's absurdist logic instead, going beyond the limit of the larynx.

Dodge explains that he labels it computer music because it's the Bell Labs computer setup that analysed and synthesised the voices, but he's quick to say that it's not generative music. Each poem was recorded to tape first then fed into the mainframe, that was then able to recreate the language using a pre-loaded archive of words and phrases. This would have resulted in a dry study, so Dodge tested the limits of the system by reconfiguring the parameters beforehand, shifting the pitch contour, the formants and duration of the syllables to radically diverge from the way we actually speak. The eight-minute 'In Celebration' is a great starting point. Composed in 1975, it seemingly shreds Strand's poem of the same name, in actuality locating its spirit, hanging on the word "you" just like Strand does. Dodge works with speed and pitch radically, twisting the phrases into machine-gunned barrages or disorienting decelerated harmonies. The words are still there - "your lungs prepare themselves for an ashen feeling" is a banger - but they've become hoarse, noisy growls or synthetic cries. 

The four part 'Speech Songs' is lighter, rooted in poems that were intended to invite audiences to respond with laughter, yet there's something even more disturbing about a computerised voice noisily bellowing out the same word, stuttering and getting stuck on throwaway rhymes. Really, Dodge hits his stride with the ambitious 'The Story of Our Lives', an "operatic dialogue for male and female synthetic voices" that we'd love to think Robert Ashley heard. There's a similar commitment to breaking down the formula of theater and opera on display here as Dodge corrupts these mundane utterances, forcing out near-songs and high drama from soap opera-ready domestic situations. With Dodge at the controls, the words shift haphazardly from recognizable to horrifyingly alien for almost no reason whatsoever, adding a sense of danger to what might regularly be daytime telly. It's an astute skewering of American culture that's maybe more relevant now than it ever was.

Our Darkness descends upon Dark Entries with a reissue of Anne Clark’s epochal proto-house masterpiece from 1984.

"As a young poet, Clark found herself drawn to London’s emerging punk scene. She became acquainted with Psychic TV affiliate David Harrow, with whom she would collaborate on 1983’s Changing Places and 1984’s Joined Up Writing. “Our Darkness,” off the latter album, was released as a single on Ink Records that same year, and became an underground club hit. It’s a singular piece of music: Clark’s lyrics, delivered with equal parts muscular confidence and unease, speak of urban alienation and heartbreak, while Harrow’s production pummels the listener with hydraulic beats and gloom-laced arpeggios. The song’s spirit would prove influential on both the early Chicago house and Detroit techno scenes, where mechanistic funk and existential despair could catalyse dancefloor mayhem.

This reissue offers three versions of “Our Darkness”: the original 12” remix, the Razormaid mix, and a previously unreleased dub version uncovered by David Harrow. Also included is the extended mix of “Sleeper in Metropolis,” another dancefloor hit of Clark’s, as well as the elegiac “Poem for a Nuclear Romance.”

“Our Darkness” channels timeless longing and contemporary dismay, a classic overdue for a little light shed upon it."

Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.

items.body:
Harking back to the vertiginous ambient sound of 2007's 'Language Barrier', Jeff McIlwain references Steve Reich and Susumu Yokota on his tenth album - his most cinematic, emotional project yet.

It makes sense somehow that after penning the poppy 'Long Light', McIlwain needed to walk in the opposite direction. Because the Lusine project has never just been one thing; since its beginnings in the late '90s, McIlwain has used the name to release choppy IDM, sturdy trip-hop, reductionist techno and placid ambient biz. Like 'Language Barrier', 'Melting Days' developed from film score work, and you can almost see the visuals on opener 'Sightline'. McIlwain uses the word "ambient" carefully; sure, the music is pegged to its washing, slow-motion pad sounds and submerged, brassy drones, but it's not entirely beatless. Here, McIlwain lets a molasses slow, almost inaudible kick do most of the heavy lifting, while a double-time click stands in for the hi-hat. On 'Bird's Eye', meanwhile, metallic hits flutter around the eroded central rhythm while McIlwain muffles his pads in the deep background.

He builds momentum on 'Pendulum' by waking up his deep, dubby soundscape with womping subs and wintery hits and on 'Intruder' curves the remnants of a voice around a skeletal, glitchy beat. McIlwain's idea of ambient music is open and all encompassing - it still belongs in the back room, but it's not just wallpaper.

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.

items.body:
Returning to Jabu's do you have peace? imprint, Bristol-based Ukrainian artist Regina Collage reflects on global and personal instability, infusing her haunted, lo-fi songs with tentative passion. It's gorgeous, fragile and deeply personal pop - somewhere between HTRK, Broadcast and Cukor Bila Smert’.

Hailing from Kharkiv where her parents still live, Collage is acutely aware of the lasting impacts of war - the severed relationships, the daily, ongoing trauma. In Bristol, she's away from the front line, but carries it with her, a feeling of "quiet shame" that grounds her latest album's subtle, minimal arrangements. Because although her voice is at the centre of the album, she rarely raises it to more than a distant whisper, sounding as if she's trapped in a liminal space between realities. On 'It Should Be Something', she drowns her moans in reverb, harmonising with echo trails, bass guitar plucks and languid riffs; it's music that won't come as a complete surprise to anyone familiar with Jabu's output, but Collage's outlook is slower, sadder and more exposed. Sure, she plays fast and loose with effects, but the processes never obscure the album's core emotions - heart-melting feelings we haven't heard rendered quite so perfectly since we locked in with Jonnine's 'Southside Girl'. 

'Horizont' is rooted in a kind of bedroom-recorded post-punk that's so slow and gummed up with noise you'd think it was some STROOM-related archival discovery. On 'Davno', her voice seems to float around a simple, distorted drum machine and ebbing analog synths, molded into casual moans that betray Collage's sobering, vulnerable themes. But she's almost in a different headspace altogether on 'I Hope', curling her words around a Hooky-style staccato bassline and anticipating a beat that never actually comes. Each song sounds as if it's a torn page from her scrapbook, not exactly half-finished, but certainly not polished - and it's this aesthetic that gives the album so much emotional weight. We get to reach into Collage's psyche, hearing her own instability as she wonders about a world that's been thrown into chaos. As she reconciles with the situation, figuring out her life in Bristol at the same time, she constructs a sound that's similarly dualistic - unashamedly displaying its roots in the Ukrainian underground while absorbing ideas from her new home.

Club Romantico salute an unsung pioneer of modern club movements, Daniel Pineda ov Nguzunguzu - a producer of early Kelela and the short-lived Future Brown with Fatima Al-Qadiri - with a handful of lush yet venomous originals plus a Kelman Duran link-up 

You can’t talk about the 2010’s club sound without acknowledging Daniel Pineda’s influential, border-smudging productions as half of Nguzunguzu, with Asthma Maroof. Along with the likes of Total Freedom, Pineda’s work ushered the freshest wave of syncopated club music from the US at a time when Night Slugs (and Numbers.) and its American division, Fade To Mind, were hybridising UKF with Latin house, Jersey and B-More club and a groundswell of virulent Global South rhythms that began to percolate Westwards via blogs (this was the salient stuff when talking about blog-era, not the fidget-house pish) by the end of the ‘00s. 

Pineda’s ‘Landlocked’ firmly marks his return to a scene he sowed nearly decades ago, swerving from the heart-in-mouth pads and Dutch Bubblers-type groove to ‘De La Mama’, a a slower variant of that tresillo formula in ‘Gritos’, via the full-bore 145BPM intensity of ‘Fuerte’, a video clash-meets-Ballroom romp ‘Heavy Fact’, and the pneumatic subs and drill clack of a ‘Quema’ primed for carnival season. Another crucial bridge of Global South and Western club music, Kelman Duran tags in on the EP’s slowest, heaviest, ‘Loko 4 Eva’, strapped with below-belt quake and hardest drum cadence bound to get crowds slapping the walls.

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.

items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."
